analysis.one_liner: Tightens the rule forcing for-profit colleges to earn revenue from non-federal sources.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with 3 cosponsors and referred to committee, where it died without ever receiving a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal rules let for-profit colleges keep collecting federal student aid as long as at least 10% of their revenue comes from elsewhere — and that 10% has often been other federal money, like GI Bill benefits. The POST Act would raise the bar to 15% and count every type of federal money, including GI Bill tuition and veteran education benefits, when deciding whether a school is too dependent on taxpayers. Schools that fail the test would lose access to federal student aid.
analysis.who_benefits: Students at for-profit colleges, who would be better protected from schools that survive mainly on federal aid dollars; veterans, whose GI Bill money was previously counted as 'non-federal' revenue under the old 90/10 rule, letting schools keep enrolling them while staying eligible for aid; and taxpayers, who bear the cost of aid paid to schools where students frequently drop out or default.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the '90/10 rule' to a 15% requirement: a for-profit college must get at least 15% of its revenue from non-federal sources or lose access to federal student aid [S2][S3].

Counts all federal money — grants, loans, guarantees, and benefits delivered to or on behalf of students — as federal funds when calculating the ratio, closing the loophole where GI Bill benefits counted as 'private' revenue [S2][S3].

Excludes the Post-9/11 GI Bill monthly housing stipend from the calculation so schools cannot treat veteran housing benefits as a workaround, and restricts what a school may count as revenue (no self-issued loans, no scholarships from affiliated sources, no federal matching funds) to prevent gaming [S3].

Requires the Education Department to report to Congress each year how much federal and non-federal revenue each eligible for-profit college receives, using the schools' audited financial statements [S3].

analysis.who_pays: For-profit college companies, whose revenue depends heavily on federal student aid and veterans' benefits; some schools that could not reach 15% non-federal revenue would lose federal aid and could close, leaving enrolled students to finish programs elsewhere. The requirement could also push some schools to charge non-aid students more or trim low-enrollment programs to meet the ratio.

drawbacks.text: The bill carves out one exception: the Post-9/11 GI Bill monthly housing stipend does NOT count as federal funds, meaning schools could still rely on that veteran benefit as 'non-federal' revenue — a partial weakening of the rule it otherwise tightens [S3].

The 15% floor could push for-profit schools to raise tuition for students paying out of pocket or drop programs that serve low-income students, since the easiest way to hit the ratio is to attract more non-aid revenue [S3] (mechanism).

Some proprietary colleges argue the requirement punishes schools that primarily serve low-income and veteran students, whose education is legitimately funded by federal benefits, rather than addressing poor-quality schools directly (common industry objection to 90/10-style rules; general knowledge).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill attacks a real, documented problem: the old 90/10 rule let schools count other federal money (like GI Bill benefits) as 'non-federal' revenue, so a school could be almost entirely taxpayer-funded and still keep its aid eligibility. Raising the floor to 15% and counting all federal money is a straightforward fix with clear taxpayer and student benefits. The costs fall on the industry, though the housing-stipend carve-out and the possibility that schools shift costs to non-aid students are honest limits on how much it would accomplish.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Education and the Workforce Committee — later its higher education subcommittee — and died there when the Congress ended, never getting a hearing or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Cohen introduced the bill on November 14, 2013, joined by Reps. John Conyers and Raul Grijalva [S1][S3].
It was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day [S5].
On January 22, 2014, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Higher Education and Workforce Training, where it remained with no further action through the end of the 113th Congress [S5].
The committee never held a markup or sent the bill to the floor, and no version passed either chamber [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For-profit colleges came out ahead: the existing 90/10 rule — which let them count GI Bill benefits as non-federal revenue — stayed in place for the rest of the Congress, and students and taxpayers got no added protection.

for.name: Reps. John Conyers and Raul Grijalva

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and let it die in committee

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred; all three sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and the Republican-controlled committee never acted on the bill [S3][S4][S5].

industries.note: These schools rely heavily on federal student aid and veterans' benefits for revenue. The bill would count all federal money — including GI Bill funds the current rule lets them treat as 'non-federal' — against a higher 15% floor, threatening aid eligibility and revenue at schools that cannot diversify.
Taxpayer-funded aid would stop flowing as readily to schools that are essentially living on federal money, reducing losses from defaults at low-performing schools.
